problem:
height[i] is the height of a vertical line at x = i. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water. Return that maximum area (width times the shorter height).

Example: height = [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7] -> 49
Example: height = [1, 1] -> 1

data.title: Container With Most Water
data.summary: You are given an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the ith line are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]). Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container, such that the container contains the most water. Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

data.key_insight: The area of water is determined by the shorter line and the distance between the two lines. By starting with the widest container (pointers at both ends) and moving the pointer with the smaller height inward, we can greedily search for a potentially taller container while discarding suboptimal widths.

steps.title: Initialize Pointers
steps.detail: Set up a left pointer at the beginning of the array (index 0) and a right pointer at the end of the array (index n - 1).

steps.title: Calculate Area
steps.detail: At each step, calculate the water container area using the formula: width (right - left) multiplied by the minimum of the two heights.

steps.title: Update Maximum Area
steps.detail: Compare the current area with the maximum area found so far and update if the current area is larger.

steps.title: Move Pointers
steps.detail: Increment the left pointer if the height at the left is smaller than the height at the right; otherwise, decrement the right pointer. Repeat until the pointers meet.

data.pattern_summary: Two pointers involve maintaining two indices that traverse the data structure, typically moving toward each other, to find a pair or range that meets a condition in linear time.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We can start with pointers at opposite ends of the array and move them inward based on height comparisons.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows are used for contiguous subarrays or sublists where properties depend on a continuous range of elements, not arbitrary pairs.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Hash maps help track frequencies or indices for exact matches, but area calculation depends on distance and minimum values dynamically.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While we maximize a value, the choices do not rely on overlapping subproblems in a grid or memoization table.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach uses nested loops to examine every possible pair of lines, computes the area for each pair, and keeps track of the maximum area found.
data.brute_force_why: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs roughly n times for each outer iteration, resulting in n * (n - 1) / 2 total pairs evaluated.
data.bottleneck: Every single pair of lines is checked independently using nested loops, which recalculates the area for combinations that could be skipped.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many pairs are checked.
Do we really need to check every single combination of lines?
Think about how the width decreases as you move inward and what that implies for the height needed to beat the current max.

data.overview: The Container With Most Water problem uses a two-pointer approach to find two vertical lines that form the container holding the maximum amount of water. By starting with the widest possible container and moving the shorter line inward, we explore the optimal trade-off between width and height in linear time.
data.intuition: Imagine holding two walls at the absolute edges of the board. The width is maximized, but water level is limited by the shorter wall. To find a better container, shrinking the width is only worth it if we can find a taller wall, so we always move the pointer pointing to the shorter height inward.

data.insight: The brute force checks every possible pair of lines using nested loops, resulting in quadratic time. The optimized approach places one pointer at each end of the array and moves the pointer pointing to the shorter line inward. Because the width shrinks at every step, the only way to potentially find a larger area is by finding a taller height, safely allowing us to discard the shorter line without missing the optimal solution.

derivation.note: The while loop condition evaluates once per iteration, executing roughly n times as the pointers move toward each other.
Computes the width subtraction on every iteration.

data.time_summary: Lines 7 through 18 execute inside a single while loop that runs proportional to n iterations. The measured evidence confirms this linear scaling, as doubling n approximately doubles the total step count (e.g., 117 steps at n=16 to 237 steps at n=32). Thus, the overall time complexity is O(n).
data.space_summary: Only a few scalar variables (left, right, max_water) are stored, consuming a constant amount of extra memory regardless of input size. Therefore, the space complexity is O(1).
data.takeaway: When dealing with pairs or ranges in a sorted or bounded array where moving inwards reduces one metric (like width), use opposing pointers to selectively prune suboptimal choices in linear time.
mistakes: Moving the pointer with the greater height instead of the smaller height, which causes you to miss the optimal container.
Forgetting to advance either the left or right pointer, leading to an infinite loop.
Off-by-one errors when initializing the right pointer to len(height) instead of len(height) - 1.
